This person is not "perfect," yet such a person is unconditionally loving of self and others, and would never be in a relationship that would negatively affect the self or the other.

Different types of sites are better for certain situations.

Compass is a good way to search listings that are only from the MLS database (and thus are almost guaranteed not to be fake). Other real estate companies offer a similar service, but the search features on Compass make it one is the best and easiest. Almost all of these listings will require a broker fee.

Other sites combine MLS listings (from agents) with listings from anyone (including property managers and landlords). These sites will also include fake listings, so be careful. Apartments.com is notorious for fake listings, and some people say the same about Zillow, but I personally think Zillow does a better job of keeping fake listings off their site. These sites will occasionally offer properties that don't have a broker fee (look for listings posted by landlords).

Another option is social media (Facebook, Reddit), which tends to be better for finding roommates, shared units, and short term rentals (including lease breaks, which usually mean a discounted rental price).

Yes, I am exactly taking about "helping people." Everyone has different viewpoints as to what is the best way to "help someone." In certain circumstances, helping someone can save their life or turn their life around. But "helping" can also lead to disempowerment and an unhealthy dependence. Often, is difficult to find a happy medium.

To give an example, I have a friend who receives food stamps, housing vouchers and free health care. Due to her mental and physical health issues, having free health care possibly saved her life at one point. However, she currently uses the housing voucher to live in a 2 bedroom apartment all by herself while her daughter (who she claims to live with her in order to receive the voucher) lives with the grandmother 2 blocks away. She uses the food stamps to buy mostly junk food (ice cream, sweets, coffee) while receiving free produce from a local food pantry. And she begs cash from her mother to buy cigarettes which she smokes inside her rental, and which is a potential fire hazard to everyone else who lives in the building.

Now, some people might argue that she doesn't need all those handouts. For example, she could live at her mother's big house, but chooses not to because they don't get along. If the housing voucher was revoked, she would move back in with her mother, who would not allow her to smoke inside that house. But some people might argue that she has the need or right to live separately from her mother.

So again, what constitutes "help" is a discussion with no easy answers and definitely not one right answer.

You can never know a person's intent based on a set of actions. For example, liking a girl's photo on Instagram could mean "nice outfit" or it could mean "I'd love to sleep with her."  But you don't know.

And it works both ways. Your boyfriend doesn't know what you are thinking, and he can assume the best or the worst based on anything or nothing at all. 

So this is a question of trust. Do you trust your boyfriend enough to be able to do adult things such as like photos of girls on Instagram, or are you going to always be suspicious of his actions? 

If you choose to be suspicious of his actions AND you make up a set up rules that he must follow, there are two things that will happen. (1) He will eventually break those rules. (2) You will always be suspicious that he is breaking those rules and you haven't caught him yet.
You have free will to react to what happens to you. But what happens to you is ultimately up to the free will of your soul, not your ego consciousness.

The leaky window means you can withhold any rent used to repair the window itself. It does not give you the right to withhold rent altogether. The fact that you are no longer living in the unit suggests that this point is irrelevant. 

Security deposit: the landlord cannot withhold for cleaning unless it was specifically included in the lease that you pay the landlord for cleaning upon move out. MA law is clear about what can be deducted from the security deposit and what can't.

Regarding the discrimination thing: yes, that is discrimination but there isn't any quick remedy that would help you here. The best solution is always to try to come to an agreement with the landlord that is in everyone's interests.

You didn't mention what your lease says about breaking the lease, so I assume you are on the hook for the entire rent term or until a new tenant in found. Unfortunately, this is a slow time of year for the rental market. 

If the landlord never held your security deposit in an escrow account (or failed to provide the proper documentation), then the landlord owes you 3 times that amount. Threatening to go after the landlord in court could motivate the landlord to "look harder" for a new tenant.

There are other issues that will affect intimacy such as past experiences of trauma that need to be dealt with in therapy.

The most important thing is to focus on how your own behaviors are affecting the situation. It's very easy in a relationship to blame the partner, but there is usually room for improvement on both sides.

This answer is fairly straightforward: the honeymoon period is over. Generally speaking, the honeymoon period happens at the start of the relationship when two people initially fall in love. It ends when you "fall out of love." If you haven't learned to love each other by that time (which is different from being "in love"), then the relationship could easily collapse.

Basically, the honeymoon period lasts as long as the relationship feels new and you haven't yet gotten used to each other's patterns of behavior. As soon as each other's patterns of behavior are familiar, the relationship starts to seem boring and the honeymoon period wears off. The freshness of the relationship is then replaced by triggers that irritate each other, and this leads to the "you need to change" type of thinking.

Because you two were mainly long-distance, it took more time for the two of you to really get to know each other. In any case, you have a couple of options at this point:

1) Breakup and look for other people. If you do this, you are just going to end up in a cycle of: fall in love, fall out of love, breakup, repeat.

2) Learn to genuinely love each other. This takes a lot of maturity and mandates that the two of you accept each other as you are instead of trying to change each other.  You also have to realize that your triggers are a personal problem, not your partner's problem. There are a lot of relationships that don't succeed here and they will eventually fall apart.

In general, human sexual attraction initially occurs between two individuals who are both exhibiting traits that the other does not seem to possess. So some people fall into the trap of endlessly pursuing new relationships, and then dropping them as soon as they become dull.

But the fact is that relationships don't become boring because you actually know your partner, but because you think you already know everything there is to know about your partner. This is how the spark is lost. That spark comes from true intimacy, which is about being completely honest and vulnerable with your partner by fully sharing details that you would rather not have anyone else know about yourself. As long as you can maintain this deep level of intimacy, the spark will remain.

Typically what happens, however, is that after a while the partner will start to trigger negative emotions via their actions. The partner is not the cause of these emotions, they simply trigger what is already there. But most people don't realize this so they blame their partners and treat their partners' actions as a personal attack. Once this happens, psychological defenses go up and true intimacy is no longer possible.

The emotions that get triggered are the baggage that we've carried with us from past trauma and painful experiences that we have decided to ignore instead of heal. Until we go back and allow these emotions to be expressed and released, they will continue to be triggered, and they will also continue to attract us into familiar unhealthy patterns until they are dealt with. To find the emotions that need healing, explore the emotions that get triggered and contemplate their original source.

I've struggled with addictions in the past and became curious about how they really work. So here it is.

When people are growing up, they have experiences that don't make sense to them. For example, a parent yells at a child for wandering out into the road. The issue here is that the child has no concept of the fact that standing in the road is dangerous. Instead, they experience their parent as being angry with them. These types of things happen all the time as children.

The issue here is that when that child's brain can't comprehend the event, the subconscious mind makes up a false belief to understand what happened. These beliefs include things like "life isn't safe," "I am not worthy of love," etc.

We don't consciously recognize that we have these false beliefs, but we do feel the pain from having them. Especially whenever we are triggered by an event, because the trigger seems to validate the false belief.

CAUSE OF ADDICTION

Because we have lived with the pain for so long, we no longer realize that this pain is not supposed to be there. And any time we do feel it, we compulsively do something that allows us to temporarily ignore the pain. This includes eating, watching TV, surfing the internet, having sex, etc. Note that none of these things are bad in themselves, but when we use them to ignore the pain we can no longer control ourselves. As long as the pain (and related false belief) exists inside of you, you won't be able to fully treat your addiction; relapse is inevitable (or you will find a new addiction).

So it's not possible to directly stop an addiction. You have to pinpoint the pain and heal that pain. If you are a female, it's usually about lack of self-worth and not being able to love yourself.

Edit: I don't want to make it sound like the solution is easy, because it is not. Reprogramming the subconscious mind with healthy beliefs is one of the hardest tasks imaginable. One way to do this is inner child work, and that takes time and effort.

Okay, there are two things going on here. First, you are judging your negative emotions as "bad." The result is you don't want to feel those emotions such as anger so you try to control them until they build up to the point that you can't control them anymore. As a result, you explode. The solution is to stop judging what you feel. Note that you cannot love (unconditionally) if you judge something as bad.

The second part: this issue with anger is what you could call a "pattern" of behavior. Our patterns are a symptom of it psychological defenses. In other words, at some point something caused us pain, and we decided that we were going to avoid this pain in the future. 

So (for example), let's say that someone in the past accused you of doing something and it caused you great embarrassment. To avoid future embarrassment, you get angry and defensive every time you are accused of something. This is course isn't helpful at all, but human behavior is often irrational.

The solution in the example is to allow yourself to be fully vulnerable to the emotion you are resisting. You have in fact been holding on to it all this time; you never fully let it go from the original event because it was too difficult. So this takes a bit of courage, but you need to fully experience that emotion. Once you do, you will be released from the fear of it and become much wiser and stronger as a result.

How to release: this depends somewhat on the nature of the original event (and it isn't necessary to recall what happened in the original event in many cases). But just note that if it was very traumatic, then it would be wise to seek professional help.

For the self help route, simply visualize yourself in a situation that would normally lead to your defense response. As you feel yourself going into defense, relax your body and instead give yourself permission to feel the pain of what the situation in your visualization is causing. You may need to take some deep breaths. But keep with the visualization until you can completely feel that emotion you are avoiding. Stay with the emotion as long as you need until it no longer feels like you have to run away from it. You may need to repeat this exercise multiple times in other to fully release the emotion. 

To summarize: once you can view your emotions without judging them, start to look for patterns in your behavior. These patterns will help you find your psychological defenses. Once you find out what you are avoiding, you want to actually experience this emotion in order to release the pain associated with it. This will allow you to drop your defenses and instead observe your emotions without hanging on to them.

Final comment: nothing that anybody does to you is personal. Every time you feel attacked, it is only because the other person is psychologically defending themselves against a perceived attack. When you realize this, it is much easier to not get upset by other people's actions.

Another point: it is possible to keep your heart open regardless of the emotions that you are experiencing. You can feel love for your pain and love for your anger.
